recentItems.title: 'Mutilated': The women subjected to unnecessary mastectomies | BBC News
recentItems.description:
Denise is one of at least 20 women told they underwent an unnecessary mastectomy at an NHS trust in north-east England.

More than 300 patients have been harmed in County Durham, while thousands more cases are expected to be reviewed, and police are investigating.

The unnecessary breast removals have been described as "utterly unacceptable" by Steve Russell, County Durham and Darlington Foundation Trust’s chief executive, and he has apologised "unreservedly".

Did US commit war crimes in Iran strikes? | BBC News
recentItems.description:
UN human rights experts say there are reasonable grounds to believe the US committed war crimes in two strikes in Iran that killed at least 177 civilians.
 
A new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, said February's missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd constituted indiscriminate attacks causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure.

There was no immediate comment from the US. It has previously denied striking Lamerd and said it is investigating what happened in Minab.

The experts also found Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during a crackdown on mass anti-government protests in January.

Iran has also not yet commented on the findings, but it has previously rejected allegations of systematic violations of human rights.

recentItems.title: Nine women found dead. What's happening in South Africa? | BBC News
recentItems.description:
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of a ninth woman's body in just two months.
 
Concerns are growing over a string of unexplained deaths east of Johannesburg.
 
Several of the women were found partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible.

Ed Sheeran, Macklemore, and the politics of staying silent | BBC News
recentItems.description:
One of the most successful songwriters of all time is facing the biggest controversy of his nearly two decades in the public eye. Where does pop star Ed Sheeran go from here? 

On Tuesday, every support act for Sheeran withdrew from his US stadium tour, following a decision to drop rapper Macklemore from the tour for his on-stage pro-Palestinian comments. 
 
In a statement, Sheeran declined to take a political stance on Macklemore’s comments, and stressed that he was not responsible for the decision to remove the rapper from the roster. Is it possible for pop stars to stay out of the political fray? 

We speak to BBC music correspondent Mark Savage about the controversy, and what it reveals about the conversion of pop culture and politics.

recentItems.title: How climate change is shrinking our water supply and other stories | Global News Podcast
recentItems.description:
The United Nations says climate change is having a serious effect on the global supply of fresh water. Rivers and lakes are drying up while glaciers are retreating according to a new report. “This is not a single bad year, but a persistent decade-long signal,” said World Meteorological Organization chief Celeste Saulo.

recentItems.title: Russia to vote in first parliamentary election since invasion of Ukraine | BBC News
recentItems.description:
Russia is voting in its first parliamentary election this weekend since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
 
The system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" - where the Kremlin does the managing - which means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.
 
The election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.
 
For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important.
 
Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.
